screens.title: Control Structures and Error Handling
screens.subtitle: Decision-making, repetition, and safe failure in Solidity

narration.text: In this lesson we'll map how Solidity controls program flow and how contracts should fail safely. You'll learn the essential conditionals — if, else if and else — and how to use loops to repeat work. We'll also cover the three key error handlers: require, revert, and assert, and why choosing the correct one affects both safety and gas refunds. Through a compact whitelist lab you'll see these tools combined: input validation that guards state, loop patterns to avoid gas problems, and assertions that protect invariants. As you learn, pay attention to the practical trade-offs: loops over storage are convenient but can exceed block gas limits; require and revert return remaining gas making them appropriate for user-facing checks; assert consumes remaining gas and should be reserved for internal invariants only. By the end you'll know when to validate inputs, when to bail out early, and how to structure checks so your contracts are predictable and auditable. Think about a simple traffic light: conditionals route execution, loops are the repetitive cycles, and error handlers are the emergency brakes — you'll learn to use each correctly.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Use clear conditionals for decisions, avoid unbounded loops on-chain, and pick require/revert for expected checks while reserving assert for internal invariants.

Starter Example
function checkValue(uint256 _input) public returns (string memory) {

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement conditional logic using if, else if and else so your contract chooses the right path when inputs vary. You'll learn how to use for and while loops to perform repetitive tasks and why iteration over storage has gas costs that matter in deployed contracts. You'll apply Solidity's three primary error handling mechanisms — require, revert and assert — choosing the correct one for user checks, complex conditional failures, or internal invariants. Finally, you'll distinguish practical use cases: use require for input validation and expected failures, revert when you need flexible control of early exit or custom errors, and reserve assert for invariants that should never fail. Each objective includes a short skill explanation and a verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a Remix lab. These skills are essential because smart contracts run on-chain where errors are costly; correct checks prevent lost funds, improve user experience, and reduce attack surface. You'll practice each item with examples and a final whitelist lab that ties everything together.

screens.title: Conditional Statements in Solidity
screens.subtitle: Using if, else if, and else for decision logic

narration.text: Conditionals are the primary tool for branching execution in Solidity. A conditional evaluates a boolean expression and directs which block of code runs next. In practice that means validating inputs, enforcing role checks, or choosing between state updates. For example, a function that sets a stored value might handle high inputs differently from medium or low inputs using if, else if, and else. This saves you from duplicating code and makes the contract's intent explicit. A common pitfall is chaining many conditions inline until logic becomes hard to audit; long if/else chains should be refactored into helper functions or early returns to keep the top-level logic obvious. Also prefer clear boolean expressions rather than nested negative checks, which are harder to reason about and easier to get wrong in security reviews. In the classroom code we use a checkValue function: if the input is greater than a high threshold we store it directly; else if it's medium range we store a transformed value; otherwise we reset to zero. That concrete example shows typical decision-making: input validation, state assignment, and a human-readable return message. As you write conditionals, ask: could this branch be triggered incorrectly, and is the error case handled gracefully? This habit reduces subtle bugs in deployed contracts.

keyIdea.title: Conditional Insight
keyIdea.text: Use clear, auditable conditionals. Keep branches simple and prefer early returns or small helpers over long nested chains.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Conditionals
Definition

Decision-making with if / else

Evaluate boolean expressions to choose which code path updates contract state or returns a value.

// Example: checkValue
function checkValue(uint256 _input) public returns (string memory) {
  if (_input > 100) {
    value = _input;
    return "Value set to high input.";
  } else if (_input > 50) {
    value = _input / 2;
    return "Value set to half of medium input.";
  } else {
    value = 0;
    return "Value reset to zero.";
  }
}
Explanation & Tips
  • Keep conditions short and descriptive; prefer helper functions for complex checks.
  • Use early returns to reduce nesting and improve auditability.
  • Avoid contradictory branches; document assumptions in comments or returns.
Analogy

Think of a traffic light: the condition determines whether you stop, slow, or go, and the contract must handle each case safely.

Common Mistake

Overly deep nested conditionals hide bugs. Refactor when you have many else if branches.

Key Takeaway

Readable conditionals make behavior predictable and easier to audit.

screens.title: Conditionals — Best Practices & Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Readable checks, early returns, and avoiding logical errors

narration.text: When writing conditionals, clarity beats cleverness. A few established practices reduce bugs and make audits faster. First, favor early returns for input validation; check for invalid states at the start and revert immediately. This short-circuits execution and avoids deep nesting. Second, prefer positive predicates over double-negatives — code that reads naturally reduces the chance of a logic inversion. Third, isolate authorization checks into small modifiers or helper functions so the main logic remains focused on business rules. Let me give a concrete scenario: suppose you have a function that should only be called by the contract owner and should only accept positive token amounts. Instead of nesting these checks, first require ownership, then require(amount > 0), and then proceed. This pattern ensures failures are explicit and gas-efficient. A common misconception is that more checks always cost more gas; in fact, earlier reverts can save gas when they avoid expensive work later. Another pitfall is returning different error strings inconsistently; consistent, concise messages or custom errors make debugging and testing easier. Finally, break very long chains into named predicates with clear names — human-readable conditions lead to fewer logic errors during code review.

keyIdea.title: Best Practice
keyIdea.text: Validate early, name predicates clearly, and keep branches short to make contracts auditable and gas-efficient.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Conditionals — Best Practices
Comparison

Early return vs Nested checks

Early returns validate and revert before executing expensive operations. Nested checks increase indentation and risk missed branches.

Early return pattern:
// require ownership and valid amount
require(msg.sender == owner, "Not owner");
require(amount > 0, "Amount must be positive");
// proceed with action
Pitfalls
  • Negated conditions that confuse reviewers.
  • Inconsistent error messages that hinder testing.
  • Large if/else trees hiding state changes.
Pro tip

Name complex checks: isEligibleToClaim(addr) returns a boolean and makes the call site readable.

Misconception

More checks don't always cost more gas if they prevent expensive state changes later.

Key Takeaway

Readable predicates and early validation make contracts safer and simpler to audit.

screens.title: For Loops: Iteration and a Code Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Understand for loops and when they are appropriate

narration.text: For loops are a compact way to repeat a sequence of operations a known number of times. In Solidity, a common use is reading or computing over an array, such as summing values. The canonical example is a function that iterates over an array of numbers and accumulates a total with a for loop. While the code is straightforward, you must be mindful of two things: storage vs memory and the potential cost of iterating many elements. Iterating over a storage array reads from the blockchain state and each loop step consumes gas. If the array can grow without bound, transactions that iterate its full length risk exceeding the block gas limit and will revert. In the provided LoopExample contract, the sumArray function demonstrates a safe short array: it loops from zero to numbers. length and returns the total. For practical code, if you must process large datasets, prefer off-chain aggregation, fixed-size batches, or patterns where users process their own entries. Also consider using view functions for read-only iteration since they do not consume gas when called off-chain. Understanding when a for loop is acceptable versus when to redesign around gas constraints is crucial for writing reliable on-chain logic.

keyIdea.title: Loop Insight
keyIdea.text: For loops are fine for small, bounded arrays or view computations; avoid unbounded storage loops in state-changing functions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › For Loops
Code Walkthrough

Summing an array with for

contract LoopExample {
  uint256[] public numbers;
  constructor() {
    numbers.push(1);
    numbers.push(2);
    numbers.push(3);
    numbers.push(4);
    numbers.push(5);
  }
  function sumArray() public view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 total = 0;
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
      total += numbers[i];
    }
    return total;
  }
}
Explanation
  • The loop increments i from 0 up to numbers.length - 1 and accumulates total.
  • Because sumArray is view, it can be called off-chain without gas in many contexts.
  • If numbers were large and sumArray modified state, you could hit gas limits; keep arrays bounded.
When to use

Use for loops for deterministic, bounded iteration, especially in view or pure functions. For unbounded data, rework the pattern.

Common Mistake

Running full-array loops in state-changing functions where the array can grow creates a gas limit risk.

screens.title: While Loops and Their Practical Use
screens.subtitle: When to use while and why it's less common for state updates

narration.text: While loops repeat until a condition becomes false, and they are operationally similar to for loops but with more flexible termination conditions. In Solidity, a simple example is a countdown function that decrements a counter until zero. While loops are less common for state-modifying functions because they can become unpredictable if the termination condition depends on unbounded or user-supplied values. That unpredictability creates the same gas-limit risk as an unbounded for loop. The provided countdown example shows a pure function that decrements an internal counter and returns zero. For loops are usually preferred when the number of iterations is known or derived from an array length. Use while only when the loop condition is naturally expressed that way and it's bounded by a small, verifiable number of steps. Also favor loops inside view or pure functions called off-chain when possible, since those calls do not consume gas. A practical safeguard is to include an explicit iteration cap or require a maximum input value that keeps execution within expected bounds. This avoids infinite loops or gas exhaustion on-chain. While Loops and Their Practical Use means use while for flexible iteration but enforce explicit caps or prefer for loops when iteration counts are known to avoid gas risks.. In practical terms, when to use while and why it's less common for state updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: While Loop Tip
keyIdea.text: Use while for flexible iteration but enforce explicit caps or prefer for loops when iteration counts are known to avoid gas risks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › While Loops
Definition

Unbounded iteration risk

function countdown(uint256 start) public pure returns (uint256) {
  uint256 i = start;
  while (i > 0) {
    i--;
  }
  return i; // returns 0
}
Guidance
  • Prefer for loops when the number of steps is known.
  • Use explicit caps or require checks on user-supplied iteration counts.
  • Place heavy loops in view functions or off-chain processes.
Pro tip

If you need repeated processing, break work into fixed-size batches and let users or relayers process a batch at a time.

screens.title: Gas Limit Issues with Loops
screens.subtitle: Why iterating over unbounded arrays can fail and alternative patterns

narration.text: Loops over large storage arrays are a primary source of gas limit failures. Each iteration reads or writes storage, which costs gas; as the array grows, the total cost grows linearly and can eventually exceed the block gas limit. When that happens the transaction reverts and no state changes persist. To avoid this, the chapter suggests several alternative patterns. One approach is processing off-chain: aggregate or filter data outside the chain and call the contract with final results or batched inputs. Another is batching on-chain: split processing into fixed-size chunks that users or relayers execute over multiple transactions. A third is to design data around mappings for individual lookups instead of arrays that require full iteration. Mappings avoid iteration by allowing O(1) checks for presence, though they sacrifice ordered enumeration. Finally, require that any function that must iterate over a collection accepts an explicit limit or index range, and document that the function is safe only for small sizes. These patterns trade complexity for predictable gas usage and prevent the expensive, unpredictable behavior that leads to failed transactions. In practice you will choose the pattern that best fits your UX and security model.

keyIdea.title: Gas Strategy
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded loops in state changes; use batching, off-chain processing, or mappings to keep gas usage predictable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Gas Limit & Loops
Problem

Unbounded iteration can exceed gas limits

Off-chain processing

Collect and compute results off-chain, then submit only final state or proofs to the contract to avoid heavy on-chain loops.

Batching

Process a fixed number of elements per transaction. Allow users to call multiple times to finish processing large sets.

Mappings vs Arrays

Use mappings for direct lookup to avoid global iteration. Use arrays only when ordered enumeration is essential.

Common Mistake

Assuming a small array stays small in production. Growth over time turns safe loops into failures.

Key Takeaway

Design for predictable gas: prefer patterns that bound on-chain work or offload it entirely.

screens.title: Error Handling Overview
screens.subtitle: The roles of require, revert, and assert

narration.text: Solidity gives three primary ways to revert execution: require, revert, and assert. Each serves a distinct purpose and affects gas differently. Require validates inputs, external calls, or state conditions that must be true for normal execution. If require fails, it reverts and refunds remaining gas — this makes it the right choice for user-facing checks. Revert is a more general early-exit mechanism; it also reverts and refunds gas, but it can be used inside complex logic or with custom error types for more efficient, structured error data. Assert is reserved for internal invariants — conditions that should never be false. When assert fails it reverts but consumes all remaining gas and indicates a bug. Think of require and revert as graceful ways to say "this input or condition was invalid" while assert says "the contract's internal logic has been violated." Choosing the wrong primitive is a common error: using assert for expected user input wastes gas and hides the true nature of the failure. Good practice is to validate user-controlled values with require or revert, and only use assert to check compiler or algorithmic invariants that signal a developer fault if ever triggered.

keyIdea.title: Error Handling Snapshot
keyIdea.text: Use require and revert for expected issues and user validation; reserve assert for internal invariants that signal bugs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Error Handling Overview
Definition

require, revert, assert — purpose and behavior

require(condition, message)

Validate user input and external conditions. If false, revert and refund remaining gas.

revert(message)

Explicitly revert with a message or custom error. Also refunds remaining gas. Useful for complex logic.

assert(condition)

Check internal invariants. If false, revert and consume all remaining gas — indicates a bug.

Practical rule

Require/revert for external-facing validation; assert for invariants that should never fail if code is correct.

screens.title: require() — Use Cases and Example
screens.subtitle: Validating inputs and saving gas for callers

narration.text: Require is the most common guard used in Solidity. Its primary role is to verify conditions that must hold for normal execution, such as sender permissions, non-zero values, or sufficient balances. A defining characteristic is that require refunds remaining gas to the caller when the condition fails, which makes it user-friendly for expected mistakes. A classic example is a withdraw function that ensures the caller has enough balance before reducing state and transferring Ether. The withdraw example shows require(balances[msg. sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.") before performing state changes and the transfer. This ordering matters: validate first, then update state, then transfer. That minimizes the risk that a failing transfer leaves state inconsistent. Another good practice is keeping require messages concise and consistent or using custom errors to reduce deployment gas at scale. Remember that require is intended for input and external checks, not for asserting internal logic. If you accidentally use assert in place of require, callers lose refunded gas and debugging becomes more expensive. Use require liberally for expected failures and user-facing validation messages. require() — Use Cases and Example means validate expected conditions early with require so failures refund gas and produce clear messages for callers.. In practical terms, validating inputs and saving gas for callers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: require() Rule
keyIdea.text: Validate expected conditions early with require so failures refund gas and produce clear messages for callers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › require()
Usage

Check inputs and permissions

function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
  require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.");
  balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
  payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);
}
Explanation
  • Validate preconditions first so you never mutate state when the call should fail.
  • Require refunds remaining gas, making it suitable for user-facing checks.
  • Use concise messages or custom errors to save deployment gas if needed.
Key Takeaway

Require is the right tool for expected, recoverable errors where the user should get gas refunds and a clear message.

screens.title: revert() and Custom Errors
screens.subtitle: Flexible early exits and efficient custom errors (Solidity 0.8.4+)

narration.text: Revert is a general mechanism to stop execution and roll back state, and it behaves similarly to require in that it refunds remaining gas. You might use revert when handling complex conditional logic that doesn't fit neatly inside a single boolean check, or when you want to throw a custom error type for richer information without a long string. In the whitelist starter code, custom errors such as MaxAddressesReached and AlreadyWhitelisted are declared and used with revert to provide structured error data. Custom errors are more gas-efficient than long strings and can include typed fields that make testing and diagnostics easier. Use revert with a clear reason or a custom error when failing a more complex validation or when you want to return typed failure data to the caller. A typical pattern is to check a condition, and if it fails, revert with a custom error that documents the maximum allowed and the current count. Like require, revert is intended for recoverable or expected error conditions. Choosing between require and revert often comes down to style and whether you want the extra flexibility or gas profile of custom errors.

keyIdea.title: revert() Tip
keyIdea.text: Use revert for flexible early exits and custom typed errors to save gas and provide structured failure data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › revert()
Custom Error Example
error MaxAddressesReached(uint256 maxAllowed, uint256 currentCount);

if (numWhitelistedAddresses >= maxWhitelistedAddresses) {
  revert MaxAddressesReached(maxWhitelistedAddresses, numWhitelistedAddresses);
}
Explanation
  • Custom errors encode typed data and are more gas-efficient than long strings.
  • Revert behaves like require with respect to gas refunds, but supports custom errors and conditional patterns.
  • Use revert when you need flexibility or detailed error diagnostics for callers.
Pro tip

Declare and reuse custom errors for common failure modes to keep revert sites concise and informative.

screens.title: assert() — Invariants and When Not to Use It
screens.subtitle: Assert indicates internal bugs, not user errors

narration.text: Assert is a safety mechanism for invariants that should never be false if the contract logic is correct. It is not intended for validating user input or expected runtime conditions. When assert fails, Solidity treats this as a sign of a bug: the state reverts but the remaining gas is consumed. This punitive behavior signals that something went fundamentally wrong. A typical example is checking that a counter remains non-negative after an operation, or ensuring that a post-condition holds after state updates. In the whitelist contract, after incrementing numWhitelistedAddresses we assert that it has not exceeded maxWhitelistedAddresses. That assert should never fail if prior require or revert checks correctly prevented that condition. A common mistake is using assert in place of require for expected failures; that will unnecessarily penalize callers and make debugging harder. Use assert sparingly, for true invariants verified during testing and code review. If you find asserts triggering in production, treat them as urgent bugs requiring immediate attention and a careful security review. assert() — Invariants and When Not to Use It means reserve assert for internal invariants. do not use it for input validation — it consumes all remaining gas on failure.. In practical terms, assert indicates internal bugs, not user errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: assert() Warning
keyIdea.text: Reserve assert for internal invariants. Do not use it for input validation — it consumes all remaining gas on failure.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › assert()
Definition

Use assert for invariants only

Example check
// After increment
numWhitelistedAddresses++;
assert(numWhitelistedAddresses <= maxWhitelistedAddresses);
Why it's different

An assert failure consumes remaining gas and signals a bug; treat such failures as critical and rare.

Checklist
  • Use require/revert for user or state validation.
  • Reserve assert for invariants proven by tests.
  • When assert fires in production, perform an immediate investigation.

screens.title: Whitelist Contract Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Live coding steps and how the contract uses checks and errors

narration.text: The whitelist starter contract brings these ideas together in a compact example. It sets an owner and a max number of whitelisted addresses, stores a mapping for quick membership checks, and updates counts safely. It also declares custom errors to reduce gas and demonstrate revert usage. The constructor validates the initial max value with require and sets initial state. The onlyOwner modifier uses a conditional and revert to block non-owner callers. addAddressToWhitelist checks the maximum using require or a custom revert, verifies that the address is not already whitelisted, updates the mapping and count, and then asserts that the counter has not exceeded the maximum — an internal sanity check. removeAddressFromWhitelist uses a conditional revert if the address is not present and decrements the count safely. The contract shows these lessons: use mappings to avoid expensive iteration, check and revert early, prefer custom errors for consistent diagnostics, and use assert only for invariants. In the lab you'll deploy this contract with a small max, call add three times, then provoke each error path to observe messages and gas behavior. Whitelist Contract Walkthrough means the whitelist contract demonstrates input validation, custom errors, owner-only checks, and an assert that enforces an invariant after state changes.. In practical terms, live coding steps and how the contract uses checks and errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.subtitle: Step-by-step Remix lab, diagnostics, and mini-quiz

narration.text: This walkthrough guides your hands-on lab in Remix. Step one: create a new file named Whitelist. sol and paste the starter contract. Step two: compile with Solidity 0.8. x and deploy using the JavaScript VM with a max of three addresses. Step three: as the deployer, call addAddressToWhitelist three times with different accounts — observe numWhitelistedAddresses increment. Step four: attempt a fourth addition and note the revert message "Whitelist is full" or the MaxAddressesReached error if you enabled custom errors. Step five: switch to a non-owner account and try to add an address to provoke the NotOwner error through the onlyOwner modifier. Step six: remove an address and try removing a non-existent address to see NotWhitelisted. As you test, pay attention to gas: require and revert refunds make error transactions cheaper than letting expensive work run and fail. For assessment, answer these: which mechanism should you use to prevent a user from minting twice? Why avoid using assert for input validation? The correct answers are described in the chapter: use require for expected conditions like double-mint prevention and avoid assert for user checks because it consumes remaining gas and signals bugs. Finish by reflecting on whether any loops in your contract could grow unbounded and redesign them if needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from conditionals, loops, and gas

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important technical ideas. First, conditionals — if, else if and else — let you route execution based on clear boolean checks. Keep predicates simple, use early returns, and isolate authorization checks. Second, loops such as for and while are useful but potentially dangerous on-chain: iterating over unbounded storage arrays can exceed gas limits and revert transactions. Prefer view functions, batching, or mappings where possible. Third, always consider where computation happens: on-chain iteration costs gas; moving heavy work off-chain or into fixed-size batches preserves reliability. These three takeaways reduce the chance of creating contracts that fail unpredictably in production. When you audit code, look for nested conditionals, large storage iterations, and missing input validation — each is a common source of vulnerabilities and gas surprises. Keep these core ideas in mind as you build and review smart contracts.

keyIdea.text: Readable conditionals, bounded iteration, and gas-aware design prevent common runtime failures.

narration.text: Finish with the error handling essentials you must recall. require validates expected external conditions and refunds gas on failure, making it the right choice for input validation and permission checks. revert also refunds gas and supports custom, typed errors that are more gas-efficient than long strings; use it when you want structured diagnostics or flexible early exits. assert is for internal invariants and consumes remaining gas on failure, signaling a serious bug rather than a recoverable user error. In practice, prefer require or revert for user-facing checks and use assert only for conditions proven by tests and reasoning. The whitelist lab shows all three: require for constructor validation and balance checks, revert and custom errors for nuanced failure modes, and assert to protect an invariant after updating state. Remember this simple rule of thumb: require/revert are for users; assert is for developers. That rule helps you write contracts that fail gracefully and remain maintainable in production.

keyIdea.title: Error Handling Summary
keyIdea.text: Use require/revert for recoverable checks that refund gas; reserve assert for invariants indicating bugs and consume gas on failure.

require()
For input and permission checks; refunds remaining gas on failure.
revert()
Explicit early exit; supports custom errors and refunds gas.
assert()
For internal invariants only; consumes remaining gas when it fails.
Final Takeaway

Prefer require/revert for user-facing checks so failures refund gas. Use assert only to catch invariants that signal a bug.
